summary: Introduces a way for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) to associate policies with groups of Label Switched Paths (LSPs). A PCEP speaker can tell its peer that an LSP belongs to a given Policy Association Group.

eli5.summary: Paths through the network are put into labeled groups, so the same rules can be applied to everything in a group.

questions: how to group lsps in pcep
what is a pcep policy association group
what is the pcep policy parameters tlv
how does pcep associate policies with lsps
subtitle: A PCEP extension that puts LSPs into policy groups so peers can apply the same policy to all of them.

tldr.problem: A PCEP speaker may want to influence its peer's path selection and other policies, and doing that through per-request constraints makes path computation exchanges more complicated.
tldr.mechanism: It defines a Policy Association Type (value 3) for the generic ASSOCIATION object, creating a Policy Association Group, plus an optional POLICY-PARAMETERS-TLV (type 48) that carries opaque policy parameters.
tldr.outcome: Operators configure a policy on both peers and tag LSPs as members of its group. The policy itself and its parameters are out of scope. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: TLVs of this kind per PAG

today: RFC 9005 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP, RFC 5440) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) talk to a Path Computation Element (PCE), or two PCEs talk to each other. Stateful PCE (RFC 8231) and PCE-initiated LSPs (RFC 8281) extend it to control MPLS-TE and GMPLS tunnels.

RFC 8697 added a generic way to group LSPs and tie a group to attributes. This document uses that mechanism to associate one or more LSPs with policies by creating a Policy Association Group (PAG). It applies to both stateful and stateless PCEP sessions. The actual policy definition and its parameters are out of scope.
sections.eli5: There is already a way to put paths into groups. This RFC uses it to say, for a whole group, which rulebook applies.

sections.title: Why Associate Policies with LSPs
sections.content:
Paths computed with a PCE can be subject to policies at both the PCE and the PCC. In a centralized traffic engineering setup, operators might instantiate LSPs and set policies for traffic accounting, path monitoring or telemetry through a stateful PCE. A PCC might instead ask for a user-specific or service-specific policy at the PCE, such as a constraints relaxation policy, to meet QoS and resiliency goals.

By using the generic association mechanism, speakers can attach a set of LSPs to a policy without knowing the policy's details. The RFC says this simplifies network operations, avoids frequent software upgrades, and lets new policies be introduced more quickly. Section 3.1 adds that user or service policies applied at the PCC are normally passed to the PCE as constraints along with the request, and a group association would simplify those exchanges.
sections.eli5: Instead of repeating the rules for every single path, you say which group a path is in and both sides already know the rules for that group.

sections.title: The Policy Association Type
sections.content:
This document defines a new Association Type, Policy Association, with value 3, called the Policy Association Type (PAT). A group is uniquely identified by Association Type, Association ID, Association Source and, if present, Global Association Source or Extended Association ID.

Before using the PAG, a speaker MUST include the PAT in the ASSOC-Type-List TLV of its OPEN object and MUST receive the same from the peer. The PAT is operator configured: the operator creates the association manually on the peers, so no Operator-configured Association Range is needed. That range MUST NOT be set and MUST be ignored if received.

A PAG can have one or more LSPs. Putting one LSP in several policy groups is allowed by the protocol, but nothing guarantees a speaker can apply several policies. If it cannot, it MUST NOT add the LSP to the group and MUST return an error.
sections.eli5: Both sides first agree they both understand policy groups. Then a person sets up the group by hand on each side, like two clubs that agree on a secret club number.

sections.title: The POLICY-PARAMETERS-TLV
sections.content:
A PAG may carry optional TLVs, including the POLICY-PARAMETERS-TLV and the VENDOR-INFORMATION-TLV from RFC 7470. The POLICY-PARAMETERS-TLV carries opaque information a peer needs to apply the policy. Its type is 48 and its length is variable. The value is padded to a 4-byte alignment, and padding is not counted in the Length field.

The encoding format and order must be known to both peers, for example from the policy configuration. Only one such TLV can be carried, and only the first occurrence is processed; others MUST be ignored. Appendix A gives examples: a string such as GOLD for a profile, or a 64-bit timestamp in the format of RFC 5905.
sections.eli5: The group can carry a sealed note with extra instructions. The protocol does not read the note. Only the two sides who agreed on its format can.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
All errors use Error-Type 26, Association Error, from RFC 8697, carried in a PCErr message.

  • Error-value 1, Association type is not supported: returned by a speaker that does not support the PAT.
  • Error-value 4, Association unknown: required if a speaker receives a PAG and the Policy Association information is not configured.
  • Error-value 7, Cannot join the association group: used when a speaker cannot handle multiple policies for an LSP.
  • Error-value 12, Not expecting policy parameters: this RFC defines it for a peer unaware of the parameters that receives the TLV; the message MUST be rejected.
  • Error-value 13, Unacceptable policy parameters: this RFC defines it for a parameter that is out of range or badly encoded; the message MUST be rejected.
sections.eli5: If one side gets a group badge it does not know, or a note it cannot read, it sends back a message saying what went wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8697, RFC 8231, RFC 5394 and RFC 5440 apply. A spoofed PCEP speaker could create spurious Policy Associations, and a spurious LSP could carry policies inconsistent with the legitimate LSPs in the group. The association could also let an adversary eavesdrop on relationships between LSPs, so RFC 8697 suggests using indirect values to hide sensitive business relationships. Securing the session with TLS (RFC 8253) is RECOMMENDED.

The POLICY-PARAMETERS-TLV needs particular care. Because it is opaque to PCEP, its parser is sensitive and could be exploited, and using the wrong decoder could produce garbage. Configurations should keep the data easy to parse and verify, peers must agree on the format, and standard well-known policy formats help reduce the risk.
sections.eli5: A sneaky stranger could pretend to be a trusted friend and hand out fake group badges or confusing notes, so the two sides should talk over a locked connection and check notes carefully.

sections.title: IANA and Manageability
sections.content:
IANA assigned Association Type value 3, Policy Association, in the ASSOCIATION Type Field subregistry. It registered TLV type 48 for POLICY-PARAMETERS-TLV, and Error-values 12 and 13 under Error-Type 26.

On manageability, an operator MUST be allowed to configure the Policy Associations at peers and associate them with LSPs. Implementations SHOULD let the operator view the configured PAGs, the associations reported by each peer and the LSPs currently in each PAG, and SHOULD report failed path computations caused by policy and log events such as TLV parsing failures. There are no new MIB objects, and the RFC says no new liveness, protocol or network-operations requirements arise.
sections.eli5: The group number and note type were written in an official list, and people running the network must be able to set up and look at the groups.

items.label: Association type is not supported
items.desc: The speaker does not support the PAT.

items.label: Association unknown
items.desc: A PAG arrived but the policy association is not configured.

items.label: Cannot join the association group
items.desc: The speaker cannot handle multiple policies for the LSP.
